Protecting Your Spine on Every Ride

Your spine is the most critical structure in your body after your brain. A spinal injury can result in permanent paralysis or worse. Yet many riders tour with nothing more than a thin foam insert in their jacket's back protector pocket. A proper CE-rated back protector is one of the most important safety upgrades you can make to your touring kit.

Understanding CE Ratings

Back protectors are tested to EN 1621-2 standard which measures how much force is transmitted through the protector to your body on impact:

  • CE Level 1 — Average transmitted force must be below 18kN. Adequate for urban commuting at lower speeds but minimal protection for touring.
  • CE Level 2 — Average transmitted force must be below 9kN. Half the force transmission of Level 1. This is the minimum recommended level for touring riders.

Types of Back Protectors

Insert protectors — Flat panels that slide into your jacket's back protector pocket. Convenient but limited coverage area determined by the pocket size. The most popular option for touring riders who want protection without additional straps.

Strap-on protectors — Worn independently with shoulder and waist straps under or over your jacket. Larger coverage area and often higher protection levels. More versatile as they work with any jacket.

Full back protectors with chest — Combined back and chest protection worn as a vest. Maximum coverage and protection but bulkier to wear under touring jackets.

Best Back Protectors 2026

Forcefield Isolator PU L2 — The benchmark CE Level 2 insert. Multi-layer construction absorbs and distributes impact energy. Flexible and comfortable against your back with excellent ventilation.

D3O Viper Stealth — Viscoelastic technology that flexes freely during normal movement but locks rigid on impact. Impressively thin and light for Level 2 protection.

Alpinestars Nucleon KR-CiR — Strap-on protector with full coverage from shoulders to tailbone. CE Level 2 certified with climate control ventilation.

Rev It SEESOFT — Budget CE Level 2 insert that fits most jacket pockets. Not as advanced as the Forcefield or D3O but significantly better than the foam insert your jacket came with.

If your jacket came with a foam back pad that is not CE rated, replace it immediately. The difference between unrated foam and a CE Level 2 protector could be the difference between walking away and a wheelchair.

Fit and Comfort

A back protector must cover from your shoulder blades to your coccyx. Check that it does not ride up in the riding position and does not press uncomfortably into your lower back when leaning forward. A well-fitted protector is one you forget you are wearing until the moment you need it.
keyTakeaways: Back protectors are tested to EN 1621-2, with CE Level 2 transmitting under 9kN versus 18kN for Level 1.
CE Level 2 is the minimum recommended standard for touring riders.
Insert protectors are convenient but limited by pocket size; strap-on types give larger coverage.
If your jacket came with an unrated foam pad, replace it immediately.
A protector must cover from shoulder blades to coccyx and not ride up in the riding position.

pros: A CE Level 2 protector transmits half the impact force of Level 1.
Modern viscoelastic protectors are thin, flexible and breathable.
Inserts simply slide into an existing jacket pocket for an easy upgrade.
cons: Insert coverage is limited by the size of the jacket pocket.
Strap-on and vest styles add bulk and extra straps to manage.
Level 2 protectors cost a little more than the foam they replace.

faq.q: What is the difference between CE Level 1 and Level 2?
faq.a: Back protectors are tested to EN 1621-2, which measures how much force reaches your body on impact. Level 1 must transmit an average below 18kN, while Level 2 must stay under 9kN, roughly half the force. Level 1 is adequate for low-speed urban riding, but Level 2 is the minimum recommended standard for touring riders on faster roads.

faq.q: Is the foam pad in my jacket good enough?
faq.a: Usually not. Many jackets ship with a thin, unrated foam pad that exists to fill the pocket rather than to protect your spine. If it does not carry a CE label, replace it with a certified Level 2 insert straight away. The difference between unrated foam and a proper protector could be the difference between walking away and a serious spinal injury.

Insert protectors slide into your jacket's back pocket and are the most convenient option, though coverage is limited by the pocket size. Strap-on protectors are worn independently with shoulder and waist straps, giving larger coverage and working with any jacket. Strap-on types often offer higher protection levels but add bulk and extra straps to manage.

faq.q: How should a back protector fit?
faq.a: It should cover from your shoulder blades down to your coccyx and stay in place in the riding position without riding up. Lean forward as you would on the bike and check it does not press uncomfortably into your lower back. A well-fitted protector is one you forget you are wearing until the moment you need it.

faq.q: Do I need chest protection too?
faq.a: Chest protection guards your sternum and ribs, an area many road riders overlook. Combined back-and-chest vests give the most coverage and are popular for faster riding and track use. For general touring a Level 2 back protector is the priority, with a chest protector a worthwhile addition if your jacket has the mounting points for one.
